summary: Defines Router Renumbering for IPv6, a mechanism that lets address prefixes on routers be configured and reconfigured almost as easily as hosts do with autoconfiguration. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: If a street is renamed, every sign has to change. This lets a whole group of routers be updated with the new network address at once.

questions: how to change router prefixes ipv6
how do routers change ipv6 prefixes
how does router renumbering prevent replay attacks
subtitle: A way for a network manager to change the address prefixes on every IPv6 router in a site with authenticated, replay-protected commands.

tldr.problem: Neighbor Discovery and Address Autoconfiguration make it easy to change the prefixes hosts use, but there was no comparably easy way to reconfigure the prefixes on routers.
tldr.mechanism: A management station sends ICMPv6 Router Renumbering Commands made of Prefix Control Operations. Each says which configured prefixes to match and which new prefixes to add, swap in, or use to replace all global ones. Commands carry sequence numbers and must be authenticated with IPsec.
tldr.outcome: Routers can be updated site-wide, optionally in test mode, and report results back. The RFC is a Proposed Standard, and its IESG note says operational experience is needed to understand its scalability when the number of routers is unknown.

today: RFC 2894 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its IESG note says operational experience would be needed to judge scalability when the number of routers is unknown.

sections.title: What Router Renumbering Does
sections.content:
IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and Address Autoconfiguration make the initial assignment of address prefixes to hosts easy, and they also simplify reconfiguring hosts when the set of valid prefixes changes. Router Renumbering (RR) aims to make configuring and reconfiguring prefixes on routers almost as easy, giving a network manager a way to update the prefixes used and advertised by IPv6 routers throughout a site.

An RR Command is a sequence of Prefix Control Operations (PCOs). Each holds an operation, a Match-Prefix and zero or more Use-Prefixes. A router handles the PCOs in order, checking each interface for an address or prefix that matches the Match-Prefix, and applies the operation wherever there is a match.

The IESG note on the RFC says that reliably informing all routers when their number is unknown is a hard problem, and that implementation and operational experience will be needed to understand how well this scales in that case.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a list of instructions saying: find every sign that says the old street name, and change it to the new one. Each router follows the list for its own signs.

sections.title: Prefixes, Matching and the Three Operations
sections.content:
A prefix is an address plus a length from 0 to 128 saying how many leading bits matter. An address matches a prefix of length L if their first L bits are identical, so every address matches a prefix of length 0.

The operation in a PCO is one of three values:

  • ADD (1): add the Use-Prefixes to the configured prefixes.
  • CHANGE (2): remove the prefix that matched and replace it with the Use-Prefixes.
  • SET-GLOBAL (3): replace all global-scope prefixes with the Use-Prefixes.

If the set of Use-Prefixes is empty, ADD does nothing and the other two become plain deletions. Each Use-Prefix also carries the valid and preferred lifetimes for the Router Advertisement Prefix Information Option, plus either the L and A flags or an instruction to copy them from the matched prefix.

A Use-Prefix can be combined with part of the old prefix. A PCO says how many bits to copy from just after the Use-Prefix length, so one operation can set a new global prefix on every router while keeping each router's subnet numbering.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three kinds of instruction: add a new sign, swap an old sign for a new one, or throw out all the big public signs and put up new ones. You can keep the room number on the sign while changing the building name.

sections.title: Message Formats
sections.content:
RR messages travel in ICMPv6 with Type 138. The 16-octet RR header holds the ICMPv6 header, a 32-bit SequenceNumber, an 8-bit SegmentNumber, flags and a 16-bit MaxDelay. The Code distinguishes three message types: 0 for a Command, 1 for a Result and 255 for a Sequence Number Reset.

Five flags are defined. T asks for a test, simulating the processing without changing configuration. R requires a Result message. A applies the command even to administratively shut-down interfaces. S restricts the command to interfaces in the same site. P is used only in Results to say the Command was processed previously. MaxDelay is the maximum time in milliseconds by which a router must delay any reply.

A PCO starts with a 24-octet Match-Prefix Part (OpCode, OpLength, Ordinal, MatchLen, MinLen, MaxLen and the 128-bit MatchPrefix), followed by zero or more 32-octet Use-Prefix Parts. A Use-Prefix Part has UseLen, KeepLen, FlagMask, RAFlags, the two lifetimes, the V and P flags (lifetimes that count down in real time) and the 128-bit UsePrefix. The OpLength of a PCO is always of the form 4N+3, in units of 8 octets, where N is the number of Use-Prefix Parts.

A Result message holds 24-octet Match Reports, each giving the Ordinal, matched length, InterfaceIndex and matched prefix, with a B flag for out-of-bounds fields and an F flag for forbidden prefix formats.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message starts with a label saying what kind it is, a ticket number and a few switches. After that come the instructions, each one a small form: what to look for and what to put in its place.

sections.title: How a Router Processes a Command
sections.content:
Processing has three parts: header check, bounds check and execution. In the header check the router discards messages that are too short (under 16 octets), not addressed to an All Routers multicast address or one of its own unicast addresses, or carrying a SequenceNumber lower than the Recorded Sequence Number. Numbers are compared as plain unsigned integers.

If the sequence number equals the recorded one and a Command with the same SegmentNumber was already processed, it is a duplicate. With R clear it is dropped. With R set, the router schedules a Result with the P flag and an empty or saved body, after a random delay up to MaxDelay.

The bounds check makes sure OpCode, OpLength, MatchLen, UseLen and KeepLen are valid. A bad PCO is not performed on any interface and a Match Report with the B flag is added once.

Execution handles each interface in order of PCO appearance. A prefix whose length is between MinLen and MaxLen is tested against the Match-Prefix. New prefixes made by a PCO are not tested against that same PCO but are tested against later ones. Forbidden formats such as multicast, unspecified and loopback addresses are discarded. Prefixes marked for deletion are removed, along with addresses that match only those prefixes. Afterward the router records the segment number, and sends the Result if requested.
sections.plainLanguage: A router first checks the message is real, new and meant for it. Then it checks the instructions make sense, and only then does it change anything. If it gets the same message twice, it just says it already did it.

sections.title: Authentication, Replay and Sequence Number Reset
sections.content:
Because RR is powerful, preventing spoofing and replay is important. Data authentication and message integrity MUST be provided for all Command messages by IPsec, covering the destination address, the RR header and the message body. This is met by the Authentication Header in transport or tunnel mode, or ESP in tunnel mode with non-NULL authentication. The router's Security Policy Database MUST cause incoming Commands to be discarded or have IPsec applied. Authenticating Result messages is RECOMMENDED.

The sequence number guards against replay, and the highest value seen is kept in non-volatile storage. Resetting it is safe only when all keys used to authenticate earlier Commands have expired or been revoked, so a Sequence Number Reset (Code 255) does both. A router that accepts one MUST invalidate every key used for earlier Commands, including the one authenticating the reset, discard saved Results, clear the segment list and set the Recorded Sequence Number to zero.

The RFC notes that at the time of writing there was no multicast key management protocol for IPsec, so manually configured Security Associations would be common. Keys must be as well protected as any other access method that permits reconfiguring a site's routers.
sections.plainLanguage: Only messages with a secret stamp are obeyed, and each carries a ticket number so an old message cannot be replayed. To restart the numbering, all the old stamps must be thrown away first.

sections.title: Making Sure Every Router Heard
sections.content:
Section 8 gives advice, not protocol changes, for knowing that every router received a Command. If the manager knows all its routers, it can retransmit with R set until Results arrive from all of them, possibly switching to unicast for the stragglers. A list of routers can be built by sending periodic multicast T (test) Commands, or by using SNMP to look into a link-state protocol such as OSPF.

For networks where the router set is unknown, the RFC describes a statistical method. Retransmissions use an initial interval Ti (default 4 seconds), doubling up to an upper bound Tu (default 512 seconds). The manager estimates the round-trip delivery probability from the Results seen and computes a confidence that all routers have been heard from. It stops once confidence reaches the target Ct (default 0.999) after a minimum number of intervals based on a pessimistic initial estimate Pp (default 0.75). An appendix derives the formulas.

As an extra check, a manager can increase the sequence number by more than one for each operation and later send a no-op ADD Command with R set and a sequence number one less than the highest used. Only routers that missed the last operation will answer.
sections.plainLanguage: To be sure every router got the message, the manager keeps sending it and counting replies, waiting longer each time, until it is very confident nobody was missed.

sections.title: Usage Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives two examples, both sent to the site-local All Routers address FF05::2 with Flags 60 hex (R and A).

The first maintains global prefixes. A single SET-GLOBAL PCO has MatchLen 10 and match prefix FEC0::0, matching the site-local prefixes. Each Use-Prefix Part has UseLen 48 and KeepLen 16, so each global /48 is set on every router interface while the 16-bit subnet ID is copied from the old site-local prefix.

The second renumbers a subnet gracefully. A CHANGE PCO matching the old /64 has two Use-Prefix Parts. The first keeps the old prefix (UseLen 0, KeepLen 64) but shortens its valid lifetime to 28800 seconds and preferred lifetime to 7200 seconds, with V and P set. The second adds the new /64. Later, a second Command with no Use-Prefix Parts deletes the old prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: One example swaps all the big public addresses while keeping each room number. The other lets the old address slowly fade out while the new one is added, then removes the old one.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: ICMPv6 type for Router Renumbering.

fields.name: Code
fields.desc: 0 Command, 1 Result, 255 Sequence Number Reset.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: ICMPv6 checksum over the pseudo-header and the RR message.

fields.name: SequenceNumber
fields.desc: Unsigned, non-decreasing between resets; guards against replay.

fields.name: SegmentNumber
fields.desc: Tells apart valid messages with the same SequenceNumber.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: T, R, A, S, P and three reserved bits.

fields.name: MaxDelay
fields.desc: Maximum reply delay in milliseconds.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero on send, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: OpCode
fields.desc: 1 ADD, 2 CHANGE, 3 SET-GLOBAL.

fields.name: OpLength
fields.desc: Length of the whole PCO in 8-octet units; of the form 4N+3.

fields.name: Ordinal
fields.desc: Must differ in each PCO of a Command.

fields.name: MatchLen
fields.desc: Significant bits of MatchPrefix, 0 to 128.

fields.name: MinLen
fields.desc: Shortest configured prefix eligible for testing.

fields.name: MaxLen
fields.desc: Longest configured prefix eligible for testing.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero on send, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: MatchPrefix
fields.desc: The 128-bit prefix compared with each interface's prefix or address.

fields.name: UseLen
fields.desc: Initial bits of UsePrefix used to form the new prefix.

fields.name: KeepLen
fields.desc: Bits kept from the matched prefix, starting at position UseLen.

fields.name: FlagMask
fields.desc: 1 bits take the flag from RAFlags; 0 bits copy it from the matched prefix.

fields.name: RAFlags
fields.desc: Initial flags for the Router Advertisement Prefix Information Option.

fields.name: Valid Lifetime
fields.desc: Seconds the new prefix is valid.

fields.name: Preferred Lifetime
fields.desc: Seconds the new prefix is preferred.

fields.name: V, P and reserved
fields.desc: V and P make the lifetimes count down in real time.

fields.name: UsePrefix
fields.desc: Becomes, or helps form, the new prefix; never multicast or link-local.

items.label: ADD
items.desc: Add the Use-Prefixes to the configured prefixes.

items.label: CHANGE
items.desc: Replace the matched prefix with the Use-Prefixes.

items.label: SET-GLOBAL
items.desc: Replace all global-scope prefixes with the Use-Prefixes.

messages.note: Sent to an All Routers multicast or a router unicast address, authenticated with IPsec.

messages.note: Match Reports, sent after a random delay of up to MaxDelay milliseconds.
